📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With his head in his hands, Joe Oltmann cut a dejected figure. For weeks, the seasoned election denier had promoted the baseless conspiracy theory that the midterms were rigged. He said he had sent the White House a 75-page report laying out in excruciating detail a conspiracy theory about how former Venezuelan officials had infiltrated the US electoral system to rig the outcome in favor of the Democrats. (There is no evidence to support this theory.) He had even, he claimed, spoken on the phone to President Donald Trump.

But two weeks after the election, nothing had been done.

In a recent development, in the wake of the overwhelming victory for the Democrats in the midterm elections, Trump has broadly appeared to accept the results, claiming the losses were the result of his name not appearing on the ballot. While he shared some election conspiracy theories in the days after the election, he’s taken very little action since.

Oltmann is among a group of influential election deniers who believe, without evidence, that the midterms were rigged and who claim to be in direct contact with Trump, but are frustrated by the president’s lack of fervor or seeming interest in overturning the results. These figures are making increasingly desperate demands of the president, including declaring martial law and ordering military tribunals.

Industry observers note that “We can walk into every voting [location] and say: ‘Take this equipment, throw it out in the street,’” says Oltmann. “We can do that … that's not violent … We're just doing our jobs as Americans.”.

These calls for action echo very similar demands made in the weeks leading up to the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, and some of the same figures are involved—though allies in the administration that once boosted their lies appear to have gone silent.

“This is a carbon copy of 2020,” mentioned Patrick Byrne, the founder of Overstock.com who claims to have spent $100 million on promoting election integrity over the last six years, on a podcast on Saturday. He also claimed that, two weeks before the attack on the Capitol, he was in a room with Trump advocating for the same measures he is asking Trump to take now.

The massive difference this time around, however, is that, so far, Trump has not been leading the charge. In the weeks after his election loss to former president Joe Biden in 2020, Trump was quick to seize on claims that the election had been rigged. In the lead-up to this year’s midterms, Trump and his administration did everything they could to promote baseless conspiracy theories about noncitizens and mail-in voting; they also weaponized the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice to target those they believed were responsible.

Days after the election this month, as the midterm results rolled in, Trump shared screenshots of X posts from election deniers on his Truth Social account, boosting baseless conspiracy theories about the midterms.

It has been revealed that on November 9, he appeared to be ready to embrace those conspiracy theories, writing on Truth Social: “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting “dumps” were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote. It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter! President DJT.”.

Election deniers on X and Telegram celebrated, believing that Trump was about to fully endorse their community once again. But in the weeks since, Trump has refrained from posting much of anything about stolen or rigged elections, save for a few limited references.

Sources indicate that “I am going to give evidence to the president today … I have a wealth of evidence,” Peter Ticktin, a lawyer and former schoolfriend of Trump, told WIRED in an interview on November 11. Ticktin refused to share the evidence with WIRED and stated the documents came from “various sources, some who prefer to be anonymous.”.

Ticktin also remarked he would speak directly to Trump about the challenges and would be advocating for the president to “nullify all of the results of the last election and declare martial law.” Ticktin told WIRED on Monday that he had not yet spoken with the president and was hoping to soon. Ticktin appears resigned: “If we take him for what he's saying at this point in time, he's not planning to do anything beyond cooperate with the globalists.”.

While many on the right have followed Trump’s lead in ignoring claims about rigged midterms, a significant number of Republicans believe that the midterm votes were not “free and fair,” according to a upcoming poll from UC San Diego.

Major election deniers are split over what to do now. Byrne, for example, disagrees with Oltmann’s suggestion to seize voting machines—but he has another blueprint: reinstate Michael Flynn, a prolific election denier, to his former role as Trump’s national security adviser.

Sources indicate that “Instead of going straight to insurrection, [Trump] uses current authorities to go inspect hard drives in 12 cities, and you bring Michael Flynn in as national security adviser, and then turn it over to Michael. Michael can get this all done by December 1,” Byrne remarked over the weekend. “If you do find foreign activity … then say, OK, I'm nullifying this election, I'm declaring a upcoming election in 120 days.”.

But there is no indication from the administration that anything like this will happen, and Flynn himself has called the election “a master class by the GOP in how to fail.” The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

#105595. Tech Report: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along

Tech Report: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1245 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that for more than 50 years, scientists have debated a provocative idea about evolution: Could organisms protect their most important genes by making them less likely to mutate?
  • In a study published in PLOS Biology, Dr.
  • In a recent development, the findings challenge the claim that natural selection can reduce mutation rates in genes essential for survival.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that for more than 50 years, scientists have debated a provocative idea about evolution: Could organisms protect their most important genes by making them less likely to mutate? First proposed in 1972, the hypothesis challenges the traditional understanding of how genetic changes arise. Now, newly introduced research from the University of Bath suggests that the evidence supporting this idea has been misleading.

In a study published in PLOS Biology, Dr. Sofia Radrizzani and Professor Laurence D Hurst of the University of Bath's Centre for Evolution examined the largest collection of spontaneous genetic mutations assembled to date. Their analysis focused on two microorganisms: the bacterium Escherichia coli (E. coli) and the single-celled fungus baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae).

In a recent development, the findings challenge the claim that natural selection can reduce mutation rates in genes essential for survival. Although this theory has repeatedly attracted scientific attention since its introduction, including a renewed debate in 2023, the researchers say their results undermine its central premise.

"The claim that mutation is slower for important genes is a triumph of hype over substance," said Dr. Radrizzani, who co-wrote the new paper as part of her PhD. "It's a really old suggestion and is reinvented in various forms routinely.".

How Mutations and Natural Selection Drive Evolution.

The conventional explanation of evolution involves two main processes. Genetic mutations first introduce variation among organisms. Natural selection then influences which of those variations become more common, favoring traits that improve survival and reproduction. This process can be compared to a sieve that separates different kinds of material, allowing some genetic changes to persist while others disappear.

A familiar example comes from Darwin's finches, which Charles Darwin first encountered on the Galápagos Islands in 1835. These birds have different beak shapes that help them feed on different foods. Random mutations contribute to variations in beak size and shape, and when certain food sources become more plentiful, birds with better-suited beaks are more likely to survive and reproduce. Over many generations, these advantageous traits can spread through the population.

However, an alternative hypothesis suggests that mutations may not occur as randomly as the conventional model assumes. According to this idea, organisms have evolved ways to reduce mutations in their most critical genes (such as those involved in replicating DNA or maintaining basic cellular machinery). Meanwhile, genes in which changes might provide useful adaptations (such as those in which mutations give bacteria resistance to antibiotics, or change beak dimensions) could experience higher mutation rates.

At first glance, protecting essential genes seems like an obvious evolutionary advantage. Mutations affecting these genes can disrupt vital biological processes, cause genetic diseases, or even kill an organism. If such changes are so dangerous, why wouldn't natural selection favor mechanisms that prevent them?

In a recent development, the problem, researchers explain, is that mutations in individual genes are already relatively rare. Reducing those rates even further would provide only a tiny additional benefit, making it difficult for natural selection to favor such a protective system.

The Mystery of Disappearing Genetic Mutations.

Another problem lies in how scientists have measured mutations in earlier research. Key genes may appear to mutate less frequently not because they are better protected, but because harmful mutations in those genes are quickly eliminated from populations.

Professor Hurst said: "We'd expect natural selection to rapidly remove mutations when they occur in more important genes, because these mutations are more likely to be harmful to the organism. This can create the illusion that important genes have fewer mutations when, in reality, some mutations have simply disappeared before we have a chance to analyze them - what you can think of as 'ghost mutations'.".

This distinction is crucial. When scientists examine the genetic changes remaining in a population, they may miss mutations that occurred but were subsequently removed by natural selection. As a result, the apparent stability of essential genes could reflect the disappearance of damaging mutations rather than a lower likelihood of those mutations occurring in the first place.

A Major Test of the 50-Year-Old Evolutionary Theory.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate the question more directly, the University of Bath team analyzed data from experiments designed to record mutations while minimizing the influence of natural selection. These experiments, known as mutation accumulation studies, allowed researchers to examine genetic changes in E. coli and baker's yeast without the usual strong filtering effects of selection.

The scientists also performed three independent tests to determine whether natural selection might still have significantly distorted the data. None revealed evidence of substantial bias.

Dr. Radrizzani remarked: "This looks like the largest and cleanest sample of mutations assembled to date.".

With this extensive dataset, the researchers investigated whether genes that are more important for survival actually experience fewer mutations.

They assessed gene importance using experiments in which individual genes were removed from organisms. Some genes are indispensable, meaning that cells die without them. Others can be deleted with little or no noticeable effect.

If the protective mutation hypothesis were correct, the most essential genes should have shown consistently lower mutation rates. Instead, the researchers found no such relationship in either microorganism.

It has been revealed that professor Hurst noted: "Analyze the data any which way and we found nothing. In neither species did these key genes have a lower mutation rate.".

What Really Determines How Often Genes Mutate?

It has been revealed that the team also examined whether other measures of gene importance could explain differences in mutation rates. These included the amount of protein produced by each gene and how strongly natural selection had shaped genes over thousands of years.

Once again, the results failed to support the idea that more crucial genes receive special protection.

Sources indicate that dr. Radrizzani said: "We found that genes producing more abundant proteins don't have lower mutation rates. Nor does the way genes evolve over thousands of years predict how frequently they mutate.".

That does not mean every gene has exactly the same chance of mutating. The researchers identified features of genome structure and DNA replication that influence mutation frequency. For example, genes copied later during DNA replication tend to accumulate mutations more frequently than those copied earlier.

These findings indicate that mutation rates can vary across the genome, but the differences do not appear to reflect a system that specifically shields essential genes from genetic changes.

Professor Hurst stated: "While we see known causes of variation in mutation rates, we found no evidence for the effects that have been proposed as a challenge to the conventional model. None predicted which genes would have high or low mutation rates, and there are certainly no grounds for a shift in paradigm.".

Sources indicate that the research therefore provides new support for the conventional distinction between mutation and natural selection. Although mutations do not occur at identical rates everywhere in the genome, the evidence from bacteria and yeast offers no indication that evolution systematically protects its most vital genes by reducing how often they mutate.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Twitter’s traditional bird icon was booted and replaced with an image of a Shiba Inu, an apparent nod to dogecoin, the joke cryptocurrency that CEO Elon Musk is being sued over.

Musk addressed the change Monday afternoon, tweeting, “as promised” above an image of a year-old conversation in which another user suggested that Musk “just buy Twitter” and “change the bird logo to a doge.”.

Elon Musk's Twitter promised a purge of blue check marks. Instead he singled out one account.

The doge logo appeared on the site two days after Musk asked a judge to throw out a $258 billion racketeering lawsuit accusing him of running a pyramid scheme to support the dogecoin, according to Reuters.

Lawyers for Musk and Tesla called the lawsuit by dogecoin investors a “fanciful work of fiction” over Musk’s “innocuous and often silly tweets.”.

According to recent reports, it wasn’t clear whether the logo change was permanent. Musk has been known to use Twitter to troll both his fans and his critics.

The price of dogecoin, which is typically volatile, was up more than 20% over the past 24 hours, to about 9 cents. It was trading just under 8 cents Monday morning.

Dogecoin was created December 6, 2013, by a pair of software engineers — as a joke. The name is a nod to the “doge” meme that became popular a decade ago. Its Shiba Inu mascot mimicks that meme: a dog surrounded by a bunch of Comic Sans text in broken English.

#105591. Rule-breaking is contagious — and good examples barely help

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Rule-breaking is contagious — and good examples barely help

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (767 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most people stop at a red light, even when the road is empty.
  • Industry observers note that A latest study suggests they become more likely to follow.
  • Sources indicate that A small number did more than copy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most people stop at a red light, even when the road is empty. But what happens when the person next to them walks straight across?

Industry observers note that A latest study suggests they become more likely to follow. In an online experiment led by researchers at the University of Amsterdam, people who saw someone from their own political camp break a rule outright were nearly twice as likely to do the same. Seeing someone follow the rule barely made a difference.

Sources indicate that A small number did more than copy. They broke the rule by more than the person they had watched. According to Lucas Molleman, an assistant professor of developmental psychology at the University of Amsterdam who led the research, a few bad actors like these can "basically take off the guardrails of the group.".

According to recent reports, the researchers wanted to know how seeing other people's choices affects whether someone sticks to a rule. They recruited 750 adults in the United States, roughly half Democrats and half Republicans, a week before the 2024 presidential election.

It has been revealed that participants watched an animated shooting star cross a row of 100 squares and were told to click the square where it shone brightest, which was always near the middle. Squares further to the right paid more money, so there was a reason to cheat.

It has been revealed that each person chose first on their own. They were then shown what a previous participant had done, whether that person had followed the rule, bent it or broken it outright, and which party they supported. Then they could change their answer. The task was repeated six times.

The experiment had no real-world stakes, and nobody was punished for cheating. Other researchers say that matters. "That's not how the world works," Eugen Dimant, a behavioral economist at the University of Pennsylvania who was not involved in the study, told Science News. Punishment and social pressure, he argues, also shape whether rule-breaking spreads.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that rule-breaking spread in the experiment. When people chose on their own, they picked the square furthest to the right, the most lucrative and most blatant violation, about 23% of the time. After seeing someone from their own party make that choice, they did so almost 40% of the time.

Small violations had only a small effect. Blatant ones had a much larger one.

Industry observers note that most people matched what they had seen or stayed below it. But just over 4% went further, breaking the rule by more than the person they had watched.

In a recent development, good examples had little effect. Seeing a previous participant stick to the rule rarely changed what others did, even when that person was from their own party.

People also differed. Some followed the rule every time and others broke it every time, whatever they saw. The rest shifted depending on what others had done.

According to recent reports, people were more likely to copy rule-breaking when it came from their own side. The effects were stronger when the person being watched shared the participant's political leanings.

Not everyone reads that as contagion. Stephen Reicher, a social psychologist at the University of St Andrews in Scotland who was not involved in the study, told The Guardian that if influence depends on who the other person is, it does not spread the way a disease does. He pointed out that people who see a riot often turn up afterwards to help clean up.

According to recent reports, to see how individual choices might add up, the researchers ran computer simulations. They created a digital version of each participant and placed them in groups of 100.

In some scenarios, the handful of people prone to escalating pushed the whole group towards heavy rule-breaking. But when the simulated groups contained the same share of committed rule followers as the real experiment, rule-breaking leveled off at a moderate level.

It has been revealed that molleman calls the work fundamental science and claims the real world is far more complex. He sees possible links to situations such as drivers speeding together, or protests that turn violent.

He also claims it challenges how people see themselves. In individualist cultures such as the Netherlands and the UK, he said that people tend to believe they make their own decisions. But "in many, many cases we are very much influenced by what others are doing.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that steven Hack, the theater veteran who spent five years on Broadway as an original castmember in Cats, then appeared as a character actor in dozens of films and TV indicates, has died. He was 68.

It has been revealed that hack died Thursday at home following what was described as “a sudden and unexpected cardiac event,” the Interact Theatre Firm unveiled. He was a founding member of the North Hollywood-based group that debuted in 1989.

“Steven was a gifted and versatile performer, a superb graphic artist and a cherished member of our artistic family,” ITC directors Barry Heins and Walter Ware said in a statement. “His creativity and talent helped shape Interact in its earliest years, and his artistry, humor, warmth and generous spirit enriched everything he touched.” Related Stories Lifestyle The Pulitzer-Winning Play 'Purpose' Finally Came to Los Angeles. But That Doesn't Mean It's Gone Hollywood. Lifestyle 'The Comedy About Spies' to Open on Broadway This Spring.

In a recent development, born in St. Louis on April 20, 1958, Hack studied at CalArts and The American Academy of Dramatic Arts in Los Angeles. In 1978, he was a background dancer in the film version of Grease and appeared in the off-Broadway musical The Coolest Cat in Town.

Hack was there when Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Cats opened at the Winter Garden Theatre on Oct. 7, 1982, and he portrayed several characters, including Coricopat, Mungojerrie, Carbucketty, Tumblebrutus and Pouncival, over the next five years.

He toured with Michael Bennett’s A Chorus Line for nearly two years and then joined the Broadway production at the Shubert Theatre for one show only — its record-breaking 3,389th Great White Way performance on Sept. 29, 1983. (He did Cats that night, too.).

Hack started showing up on television in the 1990s on demonstrates including The Trials of Rosie O’Neill, Jake and the Fatman, Matlock, Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman, Married … With Children, Seinfeld, Mad About You and Caroline in the City.

More recently, he found work in the series American Horror Story, Ratched, Perry Mason and Not Dead Yet, in the miniseries Pam & Tommy and Angelyne and in the films Thor: The Dark World (2013), Fantastic Four (2015), The Happytime Murders (2018) and Amsterdam (2022).

In 1995, he received an Ovation Award for his performance in an L.A. production of Elmer Rice’s venerable drama Counsellor-at-Law, then acted in the radio version for L.A. Theatre Works. And in 2003, he was nominated for another Ovation prize, this one for his turn in the Interact one-man drama Willie’s Son.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you're shopping on a budget, this was not a good year. Thanks to RAMageddon, aka the global memory crisis, many tech products have gotten more expensive, making holiday shopping a little more complicated this year, especially if you're shopping for someone who loves fresh gadgets.

Industry observers note that that's why we've joined forces with our colleagues at the CNET Lab for the Holiday Office Hours from the Lab video series. For our latest entry, we're recommending the best smartphones and wearables to give as gifts in 2026, with options that won't break your budget (and some that might, to be honest).

So, as Mashable's tech editor, it fell to me to name my two favorite wearables of the year. I consulted our friends at the lab and my fellow tech experts at PCMag, Lifehacker, ZDNet, and CNET, and ultimately settled on two fresh products that are easy to recommend — the Apple Watch Series 12 and the Oura Ring 5.

It has been revealed that coincidentally, both products can set you back roughly $399 (the gold Oura Ring 5 is on sale for $399 as of this writing, while the silver is $299). So, they're not exactly gifts you'll buy for the office Secret Santa exchange. But if you have an early adopter on your Christmas gift list, I think they'll appreciate either of these wearables.

In a recent development, while it looks a lot like last year’s model, the new Apple Watch Series 12 does have some key under-the-hood upgrades. It has a more durable Ceramic Shield front cover that Apple says is 60 percent tougher, paired with IP6X dust and water resistance. The battery also lasts longer, for two days of power on a single charge.

The Series 12 also offers impressive heart-rate tracking thanks to an entirely fresh electrical and optical heart sensor. On top of that, it offers sleep apnea tracking, exercise tracking, fall detection, crash detection, and tons more. Basically, you have oodles of data to feed into the revamped Vitals app. Plus, now that Siri AI (beta) is finally on your wrist, the Series 12 is a true AI wearable.

It has been revealed that I do have to mention the divisive Audio Intelligence tool that listens to your conversations throughout the day to recap what you heard. Now, it doesn't actually record those conversations. Still, a lot of people aren't happy about this one. On the plus side, the same Audio Intelligence tools also put Shazam on your wrist, which is pretty nifty. Basically, some people will love it, and some people will hate it, but you don't have to use it.

According to recent reports, if you want to upgrade to an even more special gift, the latest Apple Watch Ultra 4 is better than ever (and it's on sale for Black Friday). You can also save some money by getting last year's Apple Watch SE 3 for $249. It’s got an always-on display and a much better battery, so you aren’t making big compromises. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

According to recent reports, for my money, the Series 12 is the Goldilocks choice for most people. It’s pretty thoroughly future-proofed, so it should last for a few years.

In her review of the Oura Ring 5 fitness tracker, Mashable Lead Shopping reporter Samantha Mangino said that after testing the upcoming smart ring, she was finally ready to give up her Apple Watch. And it's easy to see why.

The Oura Ring 5 offers a wealth of health and fitness insights, but in a much smaller form factor. You can even wear it to sleep and forget it's even there.

As a fitness tracker, sleep tracker, health monitor, and AI coach, the Oura Ring goes way beyond counting steps; it also keeps track of how much you're sleeping (or not sleeping), your heart rate, your blood pressure, your blood oxygen, and even your stress levels, which are always high this time of year.

Plus, the latest Oura Ring 5 is super-thin, made from scratch-resistant titanium, and is comfortable enough to wear 24/7/365.

Recent findings suggest that now, I don't love that it costs $399, or that you have to pay $70 a year for a subscription to get all those perks I just talked about. But because you can wear it for such long periods of time — Oura says it's got a seven-day battery life — it provides extremely detailed health info.

Here's a pro tip: If you don’t know your giftee's ring size, buy the Oura Ring sizing kit to put under the Christmas tree, along with a gift card or a promise to pay for the actual ring.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, sophie has never used ChatGPT or Claude. “When I'm Googling, I type in ‘minus AI’ after every single search I do,” states the 27-year-old social work student, who lives in North Carolina. “I have deactivated Microsoft Copilot, all the things.”.

The reasons behind her firm opposition to AI are multifold. She worries about the degradation of critical thinking and cognitive functioning, some AI leaders’ alignment with the Trump administration, and the environmental impact of data centers, particularly on the water supply in nonwhite communities. Her perspective is born of strong ideological convictions: “My anti-AI stance is very deeply ingrained in my anti-capitalist beliefs,” she indicates.

Though her parents and siblings are more or less on the same page, the AI use among her extended family is “pervasive.” She worries her aunt might be “bordering on AI psychosis.” And one of her cousins, a new mother of twins, created her babies’ “entire feeding and sleeping schedule” using ChatGPT and has invested in an app that uses AI to run pediatric doctor assessments.

According to recent reports, the stark difference in opinion between Sophie and her relatives can make for some pretty tense family gatherings—something she’s dreading going into Thanksgiving. The topic “comes up every time” they get together. “I’m constantly anticipating frustration and being judged, being told that I am naive,” she claims.

In a recent development, AI has been the focus of many an argument in Sophie’s family in recent years. (She and other interviewees chose to use pseudonyms or only first names to prevent further such conflict.) At a family get-together a couple of years ago, Sophie sent her résumé to her family members to get feedback, and the same cousin who uses ChatGPT for her babies’ meal schedule immediately fed the document to ChatGPT. “She didn't ask for my consent to use my intellectual property to train large learning language models,” Sophie claims, which started a “huge conflict.” That cousin’s tech founder husband, she adds, asks snarky questions meant to poke holes in her stance, such as “Well, what about if it's a poor Black person in Africa using AI to create wealth for themselves?” And though Sophie successfully convinced a different cousin to stop using ChatGPT, that cousin immediately switched over to Claude, which Sophie describes as “a total white-liberal move to pick the better-branded version of the same evil tool.”.

Industry observers note that over the past decade, the US’ chaotic, increasingly polarized political climate has put American families to the test: Trump, immigration, Israel and Palestine, the war in Iran, abortion, and LGBTQ rights are just a few issues that have turned holidays into yelling matches and siblings into strangers. This Thanksgiving, you might want to add AI to the list of topics to avoid bringing up around the table.

“It's the latest generational beef,” says Matt Lundquist, a psychologist and the founder and clinical director of Tribeca Therapy in Latest York City. He has found that arguments over AI are on the rise—especially among families.

Industry observers note that lundquist states the problem has “created a rupture,” even among people who are normally on the same page. This is the case for Lindsay, a 40-year-old romance novelist in Pennsylvania whose family is “very politically aligned.” Before AI became a hot-button issue, Lindsay says, her family “never had a conversation where you have to be like, ‘Nobody bring up politics. Nobody bring up Israel. Nobody bring up Trump.’” So she was surprised to find herself at odds with her uncle during Passover dinner when he began raving about what he believes are the wonders of ChatGPT.

As a professional writer, she was upset by her uncle's celebration of AI. Last year, Lindsay found out a book she wrote was used to train AI models. “I was like, ‘Do you understand that ChatGPT is not a magical device? It is being created by pirating work from actual writers.” She tried to convey the message that by using AI, “You're directly harming me.”.

Her uncle was “befuddled” by her reaction and became “giggly and nervous.” This seemed to be the first time he’d heard that AI is trained on the intellectual property of real people left uncredited and uncompensated. “When I'm telling him this, I can see it's really not landing,” she indicates. “I can tell that he thinks this is a benevolent, harmless thing.”.

It has been revealed that others in creative fields report running into similar arguments with older relatives, particularly those earlier in their careers. For John, a 20-year-old cinematography student in Chicago whose girlfriend works in animation, AI brings up fears around both his own career and the future of art. He says his dad, a civil and chemical engineer who works in the chemical plant industry, holds AI to a high regard and uses it to offload some of the work of managing plants around the country, organizing data—which makes his job more manageable.

In a recent development, “It can get heated,” says John. “I'll say, ‘Oh, this is potentially taking away my job.’ And his response will be like, ‘Well, I don't think that it'll get to that point.’ But then I'll say, ‘Oh, it's already doing that.’” From there, the discussion deteriorates: “Our positions are so ingrained,” he says.

It has been revealed that “Folks under 30 are giving their parents shit about some of this stuff,” says Lundquist, who has found that anti-AI sentiment is resonant among young adults, particularly those upcoming to the job market and who haven’t bought a home or raised children. This tracks with research from Pew published in August, which found that a majority of American adults under 30 describe themselves as more concerned than excited about AI—and 73 percent of the same group believe AI will result in fewer jobs. (At the same time, young people are still using AI. Axios reported in August that 61 percent of 18- to 34-year-old respondents to its poll stated they'd used ChatGPT in the past month, while 48 percent said they’d used Gemini, and 20 percent had used Claude.).

Luke, a 23-year-old living in Toronto, states AI has become “the most debated topic in the household by far.” Luke just completed a degree in sports media and is struggling to find an entry-level job. Meanwhile, his dad, who has had a full career in computer science and web development, sees AI “as the next massive step for every single person in the world.”.

It has been revealed that debates over AI are “infecting all of our conversations,” Luke says. Last year, Luke remembers, at Canadian Thanksgiving, “what started off as just a discussion about my career and where I'm going next turned into a discussion about AI.”.

In a recent development, “He wants what's best for me,” Luke notes. He assumes his dad worries that taking an anti-AI stance could be “detrimental to my career and making a livelihood.”.

In the family of Kaleigh, a 26-year-old living in Vermont and working toward a master’s degree in social work, disagreement about AI also falls along this parent-child fault line. The anti-AI stance of her and her younger brother is dismissed by her parents as “a young-person-exclusive take.”.

When Kaleigh last returned to her parents’ house, her mother told her that ChatGPT had helped her redesign their backyard. This upset Kaleigh, as a close friend of hers is working toward a degree in landscape architecture. “It's an art form,” Kaleigh indicates. “It feels so out of touch or annoying to me to have somebody that has actual money not want to pay somebody to do something creative just because it's easier to access with this data thing.”.

Lundquist has found that many older adults are “clueless” about how real the threat of AI feels to younger relatives. “I think if you own your second or third home with a 2.8 percent interest rate and you've already sent your kids to college, you're not worried about this stuff,” he says. “And so the fact that an AI bot can order your groceries for you is just kind of cool.”.

His advice? Maybe avoid the topic altogether. “If it’s done in the genuine spirit of connection, learning, and exchanging ideas, that’s great,” he indicates. “If it’s done in the spirit of ‘This is going to be the 2026 Thanksgiving throwdown,’ that’s probably not very fruitful.”.

Sources indicate that if you do decide to go at it, he suggests getting in touch with what you’re actually fighting about. “When people are fighting about things like this, in reality they're probably fighting about other things,” he says. “The real beef is, ‘I’m mad about the pittance you and your generation have left for me. I’m mad about how the world seems to be not rewarding the kinds of things I anticipated it would and the things you anticipated it would as my parents.’”.

Intergenerational fights about AI “hang on a desire to be understood,” he says. “So Dad picking up Claude and asking it for a sweet potato recipe burns in ways that feel like, ‘What the fuck, are you not paying attention?’”.

Even scientists can't agree on what science actually is

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (804 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists dedicate their careers to uncovering how the world works, yet they have surprisingly different opinions about what science actually means.
  • Industry observers note that the study, published in Royal Society Open Science, examined 18 different descriptions of science and found that researchers rarely embraced any of them without reservations.
  • "What was surprising to me was that there was quite a bit of disagreement between scientists, including scientists who are in the same subfield," says Marina Dubova, who led the research while working as a postdoctoral researcher at the Santa Fe Institute.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists dedicate their careers to uncovering how the world works, yet they have surprisingly different opinions about what science actually means. Latest research reveals that scientists disagree about the nature and purpose of science even more than the general public does.

Industry observers note that the study, published in Royal Society Open Science, examined 18 different descriptions of science and found that researchers rarely embraced any of them without reservations. Even when scientists generally supported a particular definition, many questioned some aspect of it.

"What was surprising to me was that there was quite a bit of disagreement between scientists, including scientists who are in the same subfield," says Marina Dubova, who led the research while working as a postdoctoral researcher at the Santa Fe Institute.

Members of the public, by comparison, expressed more consistent views. They were more likely to regard science as a dependable way to discover objective truths about the world, placing less importance on the uncertainty and creativity involved in scientific research.

These contrasting perspectives may have important consequences. They could affect the questions scientists choose to investigate and influence how people evaluate scientific findings. They may also help explain why the public sometimes becomes frustrated when researchers cannot offer clear answers or change their conclusions in response to new evidence.

What Scientists and the Public Believe About Science.

Industry observers note that dubova, now an assistant professor of psychology at the University of California, Berkeley, worked with Princeton University researcher Qiawen E. Liu to investigate how people understand science.

It has been revealed that the researchers surveyed 91 scientists and 99 members of the public. Participants were asked to assess 18 descriptions of science drawn from historical perspectives, including comparisons of scientific research to detective work, a pursuit of truth, and a mirror that reflects reality.

Both groups generally agreed that curiosity, exploration, and the desire to solve mysteries are central to science. Beyond those shared ideas, however, the scientists expressed strikingly different perspectives.

Sources indicate that some researchers viewed science primarily as a means of discovering objective truths. Others placed greater importance on imagination, personal judgment, and the creative decisions involved in research. Scientists also differed over whether scientific progress depends mainly on following established procedures or adapting and improvising as new challenges arise.

In a recent development, dubova believes these disagreements may reflect the individual experiences that shape how researchers approach their work. Just as chefs can have very different philosophies about preparing food, scientists can develop distinct ideas about the best ways to investigate the world.

Why the Public Sees Science Differently.

According to recent reports, another intriguing finding involved differences among scientific disciplines. The general public's understanding of science more closely resembled the views expressed by physicists and biologists than those of psychologists and other social scientists.

One possible reason is that physics and biology receive greater attention in science education, potentially shaping how people imagine scientific research. Dubova emphasizes, however, that this explanation remains tentative and will require additional investigation.

Sources indicate that the differences between scientists and the public could also help explain misunderstandings about scientific uncertainty. People who expect science to produce firm, objective answers may have difficulty understanding why findings sometimes conflict or why scientific conclusions must be updated when new evidence becomes available.

What the Findings Could Mean for AI and Scientific Discovery.

The research also points to a potential challenge as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly involved in scientific discovery.

Recent findings suggest that with researchers developing AI systems that can carry out scientific investigations, Dubova is concerned that automation could favor a limited conception of how science should work. If those systems are built around one particular approach to research, other valuable methods of discovery could receive less attention.

It has been revealed that the study received support from the Santa Fe Institute's Lou Schuyler Seed Grant Fund, which was created in 2022 to encourage exploratory projects by early career scientists. Dubova used the funding to pay participants for taking part in the research.

For Dubova, the findings represent an initial effort to understand how scientists' underlying beliefs about their profession might influence the research they conduct and the discoveries they make.

It has been revealed that "Don't take the common understanding of science for granted," she claims. "Always ask. Always be curious about what someone has in mind.".

#105582. Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1112 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1112 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mystery surrounding a skeleton discovered inside an ancient Roman coffin at Westminster Abbey may finally be approaching a solution, more than 150 years after the remains first attracted attention.
  • The limestone sarcophagus, formally excavated in 1869, carries an inscription naming Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy Briton who lived in London sometime between 300 and 400 AD.
  • It has been revealed that now, fresh archaeological research points to a surprising explanation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mystery surrounding a skeleton discovered inside an ancient Roman coffin at Westminster Abbey may finally be approaching a solution, more than 150 years after the remains first attracted attention.

The limestone sarcophagus, formally excavated in 1869, carries an inscription naming Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy Briton who lived in London sometime between 300 and 400 AD. However, a large Latin cross carved into its lid dates to approximately the 10th or 11th century, suggesting that the person buried inside lived hundreds of years after the coffin was originally made.

It has been revealed that now, fresh archaeological research points to a surprising explanation. The remains likely belong to a prominent medieval monk, and researchers have narrowed the possible identities to two men who once led Westminster Abbey.

Two Medieval Abbots Emerge as Leading Candidates.

The new findings, published in the peer-reviewed Journal of the British Archaeological Association, come from Professor Warwick Rodwell, Consultant Archaeologist at Westminster Abbey.

Sources indicate that rodwell identifies Aelfwig, an abbot who died around 1020, as the strongest candidate. At the time, Westminster Abbey was a Benedictine monastery, and Aelfwig had served there as a monk before becoming its abbot.

According to recent reports, another possibility is Wulnoth, who succeeded Aelfwig and died in 1049. Both men are believed to have been buried at the Abbey, making either a plausible match for the skeleton.

"We have two viable contenders for the occupant of the sarcophagus," says Professor Rodwell, Consultant Archaeologist at Westminster Abbey.

"We do not know the date of birth of either. But either would fit equally well if we assume the Abbot was in his early twenties when the appointment was made and close to fifty when he died.

"The fact Aelfwig was already a monk of Westminster might favor him.".

According to recent reports, the elaborate burial provides another reason to suspect that the deceased held an notable position. Rodwell suggests that the individual was 'honored' with a 'fine sarcophagus', an unusual distinction that would be consistent with the status of an abbot.

Rather than commissioning an entirely newly introduced stone coffin, those responsible for the burial apparently reused an existing Roman sarcophagus. The man's wooden coffin was placed inside it, and the stone lid was modified with a prominent Latin cross. This may represent an early example of recycling a valuable object for an entirely different purpose.

New Excavations Reveal the Skeleton's Age.

According to recent reports, the Roman sarcophagus and its mysterious occupant have fascinated researchers for generations. Rodwell's latest conclusions draw on several investigations conducted with specialists over the years, including work associated with Channel 4's Time Team.

In 2009, the television program examined the archaeology and architecture of King Henry III's original sacristy, located along the north side of Westminster Abbey.

Recent findings suggest that the same area was the scene of an earlier accidental discovery in 1820, when workers encountered the Roman coffin and broke its lid into six pieces. The damage was repaired around the time the sarcophagus was formally 'discovered' in 1869.

More recently, Pre-Construct Archaeology, one of the UK's largest commercial archaeological and heritage organizations, carried out another excavation of the sacristy. Completed in 2025, the project was undertaken to support construction of the King Charles III Sacristy, a fresh facility at Westminster Abbey scheduled to open the following year.

As part of this investigation, human bone specialist James Young Langthorne of Pre-Construct Archaeology (PCA) conducted a fresh examination of the skeleton.

His analysis indicated that the deceased was a man between 35 and 49 years old who stood approximately 5 feet 9 inches tall. These findings differ considerably from an assessment made in the 1800s, which described the remains as those of a 'robust young man' no older than 30 and approximately 5 feet 7 inches tall.

Carbon Dating Confirms a 1,000-Year-Old Burial.

It has been revealed that one of the most important clues came from scientific dating of the remains. A bone sample was submitted to the Scottish Universities Environmental Research Centre for radiocarbon analysis, which produced a date range of 987 to 1052 AD.

In a recent development, this places the burial firmly within the late Saxon period, centuries after the Roman sarcophagus was originally created. The dates also align with the deaths of both Aelfwig and Wulnoth, strengthening the case that the skeleton belonged to one of these medieval abbots.

"This confirms that the reuse of the sarcophagus, and the associated remodeling of its cover, occurred in the late Saxon period.".

The results provide scientific support for the theory that an ancient Roman burial container was repurposed to honor an key religious figure nearly 1,000 years ago.

A Skeleton Thought Lost Was Hiding in Plain Sight.

In a recent development, the investigation also brought renewed attention to an unexpected discovery made in 2016. For years, researchers had believed that the skeleton was missing, leaving an notable part of the burial's history unresolved.

That assumption proved mistaken when the sarcophagus was transported to a conservation studio. PCA researchers removed its lid and were surprised to find an almost complete human skeleton still inside.

Sources indicate that the examination produced another clue that Rodwell describes as a 'remarkable latest discovery'. Inside the stone coffin, researchers identified the rectangular outline of a structure that had disappeared long ago. Its shape was preserved by a white residue left behind by lime, a material historically used in burials.

Rodwell believes the outline marks the position of the original wooden coffin that held the deceased before it was placed inside the Roman sarcophagus.

"Although no physical traces of that feature remained, it can only have been a timber coffin, which has completely decayed over the course of the seven centuries that the sarcophagus was buried in the sacristy courtyard," writes Professor Rodwell.

Industry observers note that together, the rediscovered skeleton, evidence of a wooden coffin, and new scientific dating have transformed researchers' understanding of this unusual burial. Although the man's identity has not been established beyond doubt, the findings suggest that a medieval abbot may have been laid to rest in a Roman coffin already centuries old.

Visitors can see the sarcophagus today in the Queen's Diamond Jubilee Galleries at Westminster Abbey.

There were significantly fewer flight delays and cancellations Monday than had been reported Sunday, according to FlightAware data.

  • It has been revealed that the robotic Progress 97 cargo craft debuted atop a Soyuz rocket from the Russia-run Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan today (Nov.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Russia's latest freighter is on its way to the International Space Station.

It has been revealed that the robotic Progress 97 cargo craft debuted atop a Soyuz rocket from the Russia-run Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan today (Nov. 24) at 5:17 a.m. EST (1013 GMT; 3:17 p.m. Baikonur time), carrying several tons of supplies for the astronauts aboard the orbiting lab.

Industry observers note that if all goes to plan, Progress 97 will arrive at the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday (Nov. 26), docking with its Poisk module. But the freighter won't stay at that particular locale for long.

Industry observers note that the cosmonauts right now living on the ISS — Pyotr Dubrov, Anna Kikina and Sergey Teteryatnikov — will unload Progress 97 through Poisk. But the freighter will then hop over to a different port, according to journalist and space historian Anatoly Zak: the aft one of the PrK transfer tunnel, which leads to Russia's Zvezda service module.

The PrK port is the best site for engine burns that boost the orbit of the ISS, a service that Progress freighters regularly provide. But Progress 97 cannot unload its cargo through that port because the PrK transfer tunnel has been sealed off, due to an ongoing air leak that was first documented in 2019.

Progress-97 is therefore "the first cargo mission scheduled to unload its cargo and perform orbit corrections of the ISS at different docking ports," Zak wrote on the site he runs, RussianSpaceWeb.com.

The Progress 97 mission, which Russia calls Progress MS-36, was originally expected to launch this past August, according to Zak. But the liftoff was pushed back several times, most significantly by the collapse of the service platform at Baikonur's Site 31 in November 2025. It took Russia about three months to repair the platform, leading to a series of delays.

Progress 97 will likely stay docked to the ISS for about six months, after which it will be loaded up with trash and sent home to burn up in Earth's atmosphere.

According to recent reports, japan's HTV-X vehicle and Northrop Grumman's Cygnus spacecraft are similarly expendable. The only presently operational ISS cargo craft that's reusable is SpaceX's Dragon capsule, which makes parachute-aided ocean splashdowns at the end of its missions.

According to recent reports, the Federal President’s latest major trip takes him to Africa. Frank-Walter Steinmeier has just visited the Ivory Coast and is continuing on to Ghana and Kenya. His goal: to encourage more German companies to invest in Africa.

According to recent reports, frank-Walter Steinmeier has visited 31 African countries during his political career. Even as foreign minister, he traveled regularly to the continent; as federal president, he has made twelve trips so far.

From early on, he viewed Africa not only through the lens of development aid and humanitarian support, but also — much like former Chancellor Angela Merkel — as a market for the German economy that has been underutilized thus far. In 2015, as foreign minister in the Merkel administration, Steinmeier played a central role in the creation of the German-African Economic Summit.

On his current trip as well, Steinmeier is advocating for greater German engagement in Africa. In Abidjan, the capital of the Ivory Coast, following a meeting with Ivorian President Alassane Ouattara, he called on German companies to step outside their comfort zone and take greater advantage of the opportunities offered by the country and the continent.

The Ivory Coast is considered a location with growing potential. Despite its proximity to the Sahel region, which is plagued by terrorism, the country is relatively stable politically. The economy is growing by about six percent annually. Germany has more intensive trade relations with the Ivory Coast than with any other country in sub-Saharan Africa, and nowhere else in sub-Saharan Africa do so many people learn German — an advantage for German small and medium-sized enterprises — all of which both presidents emphasized very clearly during their meeting in Abidjan.

According to recent reports, up next, Steinmeier is scheduled to visit Accra, Ghana, for the sixth German-African Economic Summit, where more than 600 business representatives are expected to attend. As the summit’s initiator, the Federal President will open the event together with the host, Ghanaian President John Mahama. He will be accompanied by a ten-member business delegation representing industry, the financial sector, and energy consulting.

It has been revealed that the Economic Summit is taking place at a time when Germany’s relations with African countries are undergoing fundamental changes. In light of geopolitical shifts, Africa is increasingly coming into focus as an economic and trade partner.

The continent’s share of German foreign trade currently stands at just under 2%, or around €30 billion. At the same time, German exports to Africa are rising by at least 6% annually. And since Germany’s economy aims to reduce its dependence on China in the future, opportunities in Africa are growing.

From Ghana, Frank-Walter Steinmeier will travel on to Kenya, the final stop on his tour of Africa.

Environment Minister Carsten Schneider on Monday vowed that Germany will continue to move away from burning fossil fuels despite the failure of the COP31 declaration in Antalya, Turkey, this weekend.

Speaking at an event in Potsdam, Schneider said: "We will clearly maintain our course on climate protection in Europe and Germany, but above all one that makes us independent of oil and gas because otherwise we are vulnerable to blackmail and our economic performance becomes extremely volatile.".

Schneider expressed disappointment less at the result of the two-week conference than its format, which he said was far more focussed on spectacle than substance.

According to recent reports, speaking of his vision for a format for future climate conferences, Schneider said: "Basically, I don't need so many people there. What I need are the relevant decision makers with whom I negotiate and make decisions.".

Although he voiced relief that the final document from the conference had not represented a step backwards — as well as stressing that some 30 countries had pledged to maintain the move away from fossil fuels — Schneider acknowledged that it had been nearly impossible to find consensus with Russia and Saudi Arabia at the table.

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius urged calm over reports that Russia was planning to launch a nuclear-armed satellite into space as early as next month.

"First of ​all, ‌let's remain calm, because there are reports — that's true — but ‌it's ​not clear what kind of weapons these are, and the ​effect they might have depends, in ⁠turn, ​on where they ​are deployed," Pistorius told ​reporters in ‌Berlin.

The reports mentioned Russia may be planning to launch it as soon as December.

Nuclear weapons are banned in orbit by the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, of which Moscow is a signatory.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz remarked not allowing Ukraine intoNATO in 2008 was a mistake.

At the2008 summit in Bucharest, Romania, German Chancellor Angela Merkel and French President Nicolas Sarkozy argued that they weren't ready to extend NATO membership to Ukraine.

US President George W. Bush stated he was in favor of having Ukraine enter into NATO.

But both Germany and France remarked that that would hurt relations with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The NATO summit then decided that Ukraine would eventually join the alliance, but offered no timetable.

At a press conference on Monday, Merz was asked about whether he thinks the time was right to talk about Ukraine's membership in NATO.

To which Merz noted, "If it [Ukraine] had become a member of NATO, this war could probably have been prevented.".

Merz meant Russia's war against Ukraine when he said "this war" at the press conference after a meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.

Angela Merkel defended her decision at the Bucharest summit as of 2024 as well, saying a large proportion of the Ukrainian population had opposed joining NATO at the time.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called on Russia to end its "dangerous provocations" after two Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone crashed in Poland on Friday.

Merz delivered those remarks after having met with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Berlin on Monday.

"Poland can count on our full solidarity. And if necessary, NATO will of course defend every inch of allied territory," Merz remarked.

Merz remarked Europe and NATO must strengthen their defenses.

Drones have repeatedly strayed into NATO airspace in the year since Russia released its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The incident also came at a time as Poland was hosting a two-week military exercise by Ukraine's allies.

German startup investments in fields such as robotics and defense are set to almost triple this year, a study noted on Monday.

The German Start-up Association and the Joachim Herz Foundation study predicted that investments in so-called "deep tech startups" will surge from just €2.9 billion ($3.17 billion) last year to 8.1 billion ($8.9 billion) this year.

The study described the rise as a "major success for Germany as a business location.".

"Deep tech" typically refers to developing cutting-edge technologies based on scientific research, such as AI, biotechnology and quantum computing.

A handful of massive fundraising rounds by firms including humanoid robot developer Neura Robotics,  AI drone maker Helsing and defense tech group Quantum Systems drove the investment boom.

The study also showed about 300 new deep tech startups are expected to be founded this year, a 40% rise compared with last year.

Newly found startups tend to be founded around economic hubs like Berlin and Hamburg, which are also home to leading universities and research institutes.

The study also highlighted challenges, including limited funding compared with their US counterparts and insufficient support to move startups from the laboratory to the real world.

Police in several locations across Germany reported large numbers of bomb threats targeting schools.

They said that while they were investigating the claims, they did not initially have reason to treat them as credible threats.

More than 400 schools in the southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg received threats, and more than 250 in Saxony-Anhalt received the emails, with several other regions also targeted on Monday morning.

Similar reports have also emerged to the north of Germany, in Denmark.

As in Germany, Danish police stated they did not believe the threats were credible, "but they understandably create insecurity locally at the schools.".

Read more about the disruptive incidents that have targeted Europe in recent weeks.

Recent findings suggest that the party announced on Monday that Bavaria's Digital Affairs Fabian Mehring is to succeed Aiwanger both as party leader on the federal level and as one of two co-chairs of the Bavaria section of they party. The second state co-chair still needs to be decided.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has inisted that NATO was ready to defend itself in the face of potential Russian threats against any of its member states.

"We will always defend every inch of our NATO territory," Wadephul noted at the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin.

His comments come after three Russian projectiles violated Polish airspace on Friday and crashed in the southeast of the country.

Wadephul is attending the NATO assembly in Berlin and DW has   a dedicated blog on those talks  where you can read all about how Russia's war in Ukraine is taking center stage for the defense alliance.

Sources indicate that A massive strike is underway in Germany hitting major car brands another manufacturing factors. Metal and electrical workers are demanding better pay ahead of upcoming wage talks later this week. The strike has been initiated by IG Metall, Germany’s biggest and most powerful union.

Famous car brands Mercedes and BMW  were affected as was an Opel plant, which is part of the international Stellantis group.

Sources indicate that the strikes began on Friday and are due to continue until Tuesday. Wage negotiations are then set to continue on Wednesday with another round of collective bargaining for some 3.7 million workers across the sector.

The union is demanding a pay rise of 5% over one year while the employers association, Gesamtmetall, has offered a one-time payment and a pay increase of 1.3%.

The tough struggle over wages comes as especially the German car industry is facing serious headwinds because of higher energy prices, US tariffs and mounting Chinese competition.

A German investigative media report published on Monday claims that Russia would be able to launch a nuclear-armed satellite, called Sputnik-S, into orbit within the space of about 60 days if it wished.

The report from public broadcasters WDR, NDR and the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper, cites a warning from German and other western intelligence agencies that it notes was circulated at the start of November.

It remarked that a launch "could" take place by December, without quoting the document or clarifying whether it was talking only about a Russian capability, or a more firm intention.

The report stated the satellite itself had been built several years ago and was being stored in the Moscow area.

German authorities did not respond to requests for comment on the record while the Russian Embassy in Berlin stated the claims were part of a "propaganda" campaign.

The report matches longstanding warnings, mainly but not exclusively from the US, that Russia could be preparing a nuclear strike in Earth orbit designed to take out a large number of satellites.

This could have a severe impact on intelligence, communications, logisticts, navigation and other key services.

Russia's war in Ukraine, and the Ukrainian military's reliance on the Starlink satellite internet service, has provided an additional reminder of the strategic significance of satellites in orbit.

Industry observers note that german exports to Africa have reached a new record. That’s according to a fresh study just as the country's president embarks on a trip to several African countries.

Exports are expected to rise by 6% in 2026 to reach about 30 billion euros ($33bn).

What’s behind the growing demand are especially orders from South Africa, Egypt, Tunisia, Nigeria, Angola and Kenya — countries where inflation has been dropping and exchange rates are more stable.

The biggest single export at the moment is a high-speed train network to Egypt. Other main exports include electrical equipment, optical instruments, plastics and pharmaceuticals, as well as food products, including dairy goods, cereals and baked goods.

The data is being reported by the Reuters news agency, based on the government-owned agency Germany Trade & Invest (GTAI), which promotes foreign trade and investment in Germany.

In 2025, exports to Africa had risen by 8% while in 2024 it had gone down.

The Germangovernment has blamed oil and gas-producing nations for the COP climate conference ending without an agreement.

According to recent reports, "The oil and gas industry is still dragging its feet," German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider noted after the UN climate talks had failed on Sunday. "Some oil-producing nations realize that the situation is becoming serious for them — that is why they are blocking it so vehemently," saidSchneider.

Almost two days into overtime, the COP31 climate talks in Turkey ended on Sunday as many countries, including the EU, rejected a final declaration.

Sources indicate that major sticking points at the summit included a commitment to accelerate global electrification and whether or not to explicitly mention prepares to phase out fossil fuels. The suggested final declaration put forward by the COP presidency did not mention fossil fuels and according to critics would have undermined the shift away from fossil fuels.

"I understand that this poses a threat to the business model of those countries that sell us oil and gas. But electrification will make the world a more peaceful and stable place," Schneider said.

The inability to agree on a final declaration comes as climate change is increasingly linked to worsening heatwaves, floods and other natural catastrophes.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier begins a five-day trip to Africa that will take him to Ivory Coast, Ghana and Kenya with a focus on economic cooperation and the training of skilled workers.

According to recent reports, he begins in Abidjan, where he is due to meet Ivorian President Alassane Ouattara. Steinmeier will also visit a vocational college and the International Academy for Counter-Terrorism before travelling on to Ghana.

In the capital Accra on Tuesday, he is set to open the German-African Business Summit, which according to its website, "brings together senior business executives, policymakers, investors, and industry leaders from across Germany and Africa.".

His final stop will be Kenya, where he will meet President William Ruto in Nairobi on Wednesday.

The German president is traveling with a German business delegation and wants to encourage closer economic ties and greater investment in Africa.

The trip is his 11th to sub-Saharan Africa and his final one as president as his term in office due to end next March.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Being a member of Capitol society in Panem is an honor not to be taken lightly, at least if you’re Drusilla Sickle, played by screen legend Glenn Close in “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.”.

In the book, Drusilla is the cruel and vain escort for Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) and the rest of the District 12 tributes in the 50th Hunger Games, where she uses over-the-top fashion to broadcast her social status. Close worked closely with costume designer Bina Daigeler and hair, makeup and prosthetics designer Natalie MacGowan Spencer to ensure the character translated properly from Suzanne Collins’ bestselling prequel novel to the screen. Related Stories ‘52 Blue’ Director on How Lionel Messi Fandom Inspired World Cup Film: 'People Will Die for These Players' Men’s Wearhouse Kicks Off Black Friday With Designer Discounts on Suits and Tuxedos -- Just in Time For Awards Season.

One challenge Daigeler faced was meeting Close’s request that each outfit felt connected, creating a through line that explained why Drusilla changes from one look to the next. Despite the drastic differences between each outfit, Daigeler established continuity through the character’s accessories, most notably a collection of gold medals and military-inspired epaulets that created a sense of authority.

“She wears all these medals, because somehow she thinks she is the top general of the capital,” Daigeler tells Variety.

And, not dissimilar to red-bottomed Louboutin shoes, Daigeler gave Drusilla dramatically long black nails that were painted red underneath to show her abundant wealth.

The character’s Capitol allegiance also went beyond her wardrobe, with Spencer overseeing her hair and makeup. While creating the looks, Spencer relied heavily on Collins’ source material to remain faithful to the author’s vision. Collins describes Drusilla as having implanted tabs that pull the skin on her face back, which Spencer wanted to honor. But because there wasn’t enough time each morning for an extensive prosthetics process, Spencer turned to Hollywood tape to tightly pull Close’s skin back, creating a distorted appearance. She later added tabs on the sides of Close’s face to complete the illusion, along with fake teeth that heightened Drusilla’s “scary” and “eerie” appearance.

“[Glenn] really wanted to pull it so taut that it changed all of her facial features, which it really did,” Spencer tells Variety.

Daigeler and Spencer’s shared mission: to create visuals that resonate with the franchise’s devoted fans — who “know their stuff inside out,” Spencer quips. “They’re so passionate.” When the book was released and casting announcements began rolling out, Spencer would regularly check social media to see what fans envisioned for the adaptation and what details they hoped to see on screen.

Below, Spencer and Daigeler break down the process of creating each of Drusilla’s costumes, hair and makeup, as well as the inspiration behind each look.

According to recent reports, drusilla makes her grand entrance at the District 12 reaping, wheeled into the frame wearing a bold yellow ensemble. The outfit is a stark contrast to the muted colors worn throughout Panem’s poorest district — the exact irony Spencer and Daigeler hoped to portray by making that the character’s brightest look in the film.

According to recent reports, “It shouldn’t have any practicality. That is why she was driven in,” Daigeler says of the tightly-cinched yellow coat dress. “It was supposed to be very stiff.”.

In a recent development, to complement the dress’ high collar, Spencer styled Close with an orange bob that also paid homage to the film’s ‘70s aesthetic. At Close’s request, the look was completed with a raven headpiece — which, to be clear, was not an intentional nod to Lenore Dove’s name poem.

“For me, that sort of represents the children of the district — something that’s taxidermied and dead on their head,” Spencer indicates about the headpiece. “And [Drusilla’s] so proud of that statement.”.

In a recent development, black medals and military-inspired shoulder plates further accentuated the ensemble, reinforcing Drusilla’s self-appointed authority. “She looked like a yellow general,” Daigeler adds.

In a recent development, when representing District 12 at the Capitol’s chariot parade, Drusilla’s color palette dims to an all-black look that publicly links her to the district’s coal-mining industry. To elevate the outfit and solidify her Capitol status, Daigeler experimented with different textures to create the illusion of leatherlike skin while also keeping her gold medals and fringed military epaulets.

Recent findings suggest that “We wanted to give it strength,” Daigeler claims of the outfit, which, she notes, also signals that things are getting more serious in the film’s storyline. “We wanted it to be a little bit aggressive and very demanding. And very Capitol.”.

In a recent development, close initially wanted to style the look with an extravagant, fluffy hat, but she and Spencer ultimately settled on a simpler black wig with pointed horns so as not to distract from Drusilla’s face. The shorter bangs draw more attention to the exaggerated eye makeup and the face-slimming tabs.

Drusilla settles on a softer green dress for the tributes’ interviews with Caesar Flickerman (Kieran Culkin), which once again challenged Daigeler to maintain the character’s threads between outfit changes.

In a recent development, “Where’s the strength? Where’s the craziness?” she asked herself when accessorizing Drusilla’s third look, a crepey, olive-hued gown with a high neck and massive, billowy sleeves.

This time, Daigeler forwent Drusilla’s medallions and instead made a statement by adding red gloves, tights and boots, paired with spiky necklaces.

It has been revealed that spencer leaned further into the softer ensemble by adding a wave to Drusilla’s hair, washed with a light shade of pink. “I really like fabrics and the colors and how the hair and makeup is going to be one big look altogether,” Spencer notes.

Drusilla’s final appearance comes after Haymitch is declared the victor of the 50th Hunger Games — or, at least in Drusilla’s mind, after she is declared the victor. Complete with a purple sash, the look was designed to make it seem as if Drusilla herself had won the games.

Industry observers note that this was the only outfit not described in Collins’ novel, giving Daigeler the creative freedom to execute her own vision. Knowing Drusilla would appear on the colorful stage, she wanted to put her in a bold red ensemble that would ensure she stood out.

Without a predetermined silhouette in mind, Daigeler drew inspiration from designers Alexander McQueen, Talyano and Balenciaga, as well as Renaissance-era shapes.

In a recent development, “I went to a beautiful fabric store in London, and I just found all these beautiful, different textured red fabrics,” Daigeler claims. “I didn’t have it clear what would be the silhouette of the dress, but I knew that it should be an evening gown and somehow huge and over the top.”.

Spencer completed the transformation by leaning into the showgirl-inspired makeup, settling on a bright red lip and feathered hair.

Recent findings suggest that “[Drusilla’s] like a performer. When you really do think about it, she’s a narcissist. ‘This is me. I’m bold. I’m dominant,’” Spencer states. “We had all the showgirls — all of those substantial colors and the feathers and everything else, so it’s almost like a carnival of entertainers coming together on the stage. #105577. Tech Report: Two massive stars may be secretly feeding the Milky Way’s supermassive black hole
